messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 73-year-old divorced journalist from North America, has been struggling with intense and persistent symptoms following his involvement in a man-made disaster several years ago. The event was deeply traumatic, leaving him with vivid memories that feel almost surreal and replayed constantly like a film on loop. One of the most potent triggers for John is the taste of hazelnuts, which he associates strongly with the disaster. This gustatory trigger has become so powerful that even the slightest whiff of it in any unpredictable situation causes him to freeze completely and retreat into a state of extreme vigilance. The unpredictability of daily life makes this particularly challenging, as he constantly feels on edge. John’s triggers have significantly shaped his maladaptive strategies. He always sits with his back against a wall when he is out, ensuring that he can see everything around him. This behavior has become so ingrained that it affects his professional life; he often avoids social events or meetings where seating arrangements are not to his liking. Additionally, John has developed an impulse to spend money compulsively as a way of distracting himself from the overwhelming thoughts and feelings associated with the trauma. The intrusive memories are another major component of John’s distress. He relives the event vividly when these memories surface, which happens frequently and unpredictably. This memory replay not only reinforces his sense of threat but also fuels his negative appraisals about the world and himself. The intensity of these intrusions has made him believe that he will never be able to handle thinking about the event again and that nothing in life feels meaningful anymore. John’s belief that the trauma makes it impossible for him to feel normal emotions is deeply entrenched, which drives his maladaptive behaviors further. He spends impulsively as a way to numb himself from the emotional pain and anxiety. This spending pattern has led to significant financial strain but remains an important coping mechanism for him. The memory replay also feeds into John’s perception of threat. When he relives the event, he listens intently for any sounds that might indicate someone is entering his home, even though he knows rationally that he is safe. The intensity and frequency of these memories make it impossible for him to relax, despite his awareness of being in a secure environment. John's constant vigilance has also made him highly attuned to potential threats or weapons in any setting. This hyper-awareness of danger is particularly acute when he encounters visual triggers such as photographs related to the disaster. These images often lead to intense flashbacks and further reinforce his belief that he cannot handle thinking about the event without feeling overwhelmed. The cycle is tightly wound: John’s memories fuel his sense of threat, which in turn exacerbates his maladaptive strategies like compulsive spending and sitting with his back against a wall for constant visibility. Each component feeds into the next, creating a self-reinforcing loop that has become increasingly difficult to break. What finally brought John to seek help was an incident where he froze completely during a critical assignment at work, unable to perform because of a sudden flashback triggered by the taste of hazelnuts. He realized then that his ability to function both professionally and personally was severely compromised. Despite his fears about revisiting the trauma, he hopes for some relief from the overwhelming anxiety and despair that have taken over his life. John’s current state is marked by a profound sense of hopelessness and a deep desire to regain control over his thoughts and emotions. He is terrified of being unable to cope with the memories but also desperate to find a way out of this cycle of fear and avoidance.
